blocks.text: Jenny went around Daniel’s shuttered building and down the steps into the sunken service yard. The upstairs laboratory looked as empty as it had after the police search. Below it, the service door stood open. Daniel had cleaned a path from that door to the workbench. Everything that had been on the floor now leaned against something else.
Jenny stepped over a cable and checked the clock above the sink. Billy knew the address. He expected her call in an hour.
“Miss Jenkins.” Daniel spread his arms. “Welcome.”
Jenny remembered him beside the giant robot, barking orders while it tore through the street. Seeing him offer a polite welcome across a laboratory bench did not make that memory any less clear.
“Dr. Orkleson. This is quite a departure from killer robots.”
Daniel’s arms lowered. “That robot was an unfortunate incident.”
“That’s one way to describe it.”
He straightened his coat. “I owe this city for the damage. Free energy would be a way to give something back.”
Jenny opened her notebook. “And you’re doing that through Eleanor Blackwell’s campaign?”
“She recognizes the value of my work.” He glanced toward the rear workshop. “The robot got a mind of its own. It was never supposed to behave that way.”
“You were standing beside it giving orders.”
“Trying to bring it under control.” His fingers tightened against the edge of the bench. “Thank goodness for those Defenders.”
He delivered the last words through gritted teeth. Jenny watched him force his mouth back into a smile.
“So what’s your official role in her campaign? Technical adviser?”
“I prefer director of research.”
“Then let’s start with the research.”
Daniel guided her to four lightbulbs mounted on a board. A cable disappeared beneath the bench into a metal casing. He turned a switch. The bulbs glowed.
Jenny waited. Daniel waited for her to say something.
“Those are lights,” she said.
“Powered by an experimental system.”
“What powers the system?”
“That is the part still under development.”
She wrote it down. “How long will they stay on?”
“Long enough for you to see that it works.”
“And how many homes can it supply?”
“With the proper equipment, the potential is extraordinary.”
Jenny looked beneath the bench. “Is that a battery?”
“A storage unit. Today I’m showing you how we’ll use the power. The source comes later.”
“So you’re showing me that stored electricity can light four bulbs.”
blocks.alt: Civilian reporter Jenny looks unimpressed as Daniel proudly demonstrates four ordinary lightbulbs on his laboratory bench.

blocks.text: Daniel’s smile became smaller. “You’re seeing the beginning.”
“People are hearing that you can power Cleveland.”
He switched off the lights. “Perhaps the larger apparatus will help you appreciate the scale.”
Something moved behind his shoulder. A blond head drifted from behind a cabinet beside the front-room bench, iron teeth catching the lamplight.
Jenny knew those jaws. Her pencil stopped against the page.
Luke glanced at her notebook. “Is she writing about me?”
“Not today,” Daniel said.
Jenny made herself look back at the scientist. “What happened to him?”
“A medical matter.”
“You could ask me. I’m right here,” Luke said.
“And you can let me finish.” Daniel pointed back toward the cabinet. “Wait over there.”
Luke’s eyes narrowed, but he drifted away. He had looked at Jenny as though she were another visitor. Nothing in his expression suggested he knew who had faced him in pink.
She kept her pencil moving. “Does your electricity project have something to do with his treatment?”
“Many applications are possible.”
“Does Eleanor know that?”
Daniel rolled a tall shelf away from the wall and opened the workshop door behind it. “This way.”

The workshop behind the basement’s storage shelves smelled of oil and old dust. A small window high in the outer wall looked into the sunken yard. A large empty cylinder stood behind a partition, its cables running toward a switchboard. Beside it, two tall shapes were covered with sheets.
Jenny stopped near the doorway. A metal cuff protruded beneath one sheet. It was wide enough for a wrist.
“What’s under there?”
“Testing equipment.”
“Why does it need restraints?”
“Safety.”
“For whom?”
Daniel lifted the edge of the sheet and let it fall again. “You came to discuss electricity.”
“I did. You haven’t told me where it comes from.” Jenny closed her notebook. “I’ll put my questions in writing. You can send the answers to the newsroom.”
She turned toward the outer door.
“One final demonstration,” Daniel said. “Then you’ll have something worth printing.”
A heavy latch snapped shut inside the service door. Jenny reached it and pulled the handle. It did not turn.
She looked back toward the workshop. Daniel had stepped through a narrow door into the control booth behind the glass partition. Luke hovered beside him.
“Open it,” Jenny said.
Daniel put his hand on a switch.
A thin hiss came from the wall. Jenny felt cool air against her cheek and breathed in before she understood. Pale wisps curled from the vents.
She pulled her sleeve over her mouth. She had to get out, even if they saw how fast she could move. She turned toward the control booth, looking for another way through.
blocks.alt: Jenny covers her mouth with her blouse sleeve and reaches for the locked laboratory door as gas escapes from wall vents; Daniel and a worried Luke watch from behind glass.

blocks.text: Then her knees softened.

She tried to push off, but her foot caught the cable she had stepped over on the way in. The room tilted. She grabbed the outer door’s handle to keep herself upright. Her notebook slid across the floor.
Daniel watched her stumble. “Still trying to get out.”
Luke pressed closer to the glass. “You said an interview.”
“She had one.”
Jenny tried to shout. Her sleeve fell away from her face. The last thing she saw was Luke turning toward his uncle.
When she opened her eyes, the gas was gone. The room hummed with machinery.

She tried to lift a hand. Steel held her wrist against an armrest. Her other wrist was secured too, and broad cuffs closed around her ankles. The sheet lay folded on the floor beneath the angled metal chair.
Daniel stood at the switchboard with her notebook. Luke hovered above his shoulder. Behind them, the second station was empty.
blocks.alt: Jenny, still dressed in her civilian white blouse and pink skirt, sits restrained at the wrists and ankles in an angled metal station while Daniel holds her notebook and Luke watches uneasily. The adjacent station is empty.

blocks.text: “Let me out,” Jenny said. Her voice sounded thick.
“You’ll feel better shortly.”
“Then undo these.”
Daniel turned a page without looking up. “In a little while.”
She tested the cuffs without jerking them. No slack. Her legs still felt heavy. Speed would not take her through steel, and showing what she could do would give him another reason to keep her there.
“Billy knows where I am.”
“I’m counting on it.”
Jenny looked through the workshop doorway toward the clock above the sink. She could not read its hands from the chair.
“He’ll bring the police.”
“Or someone more useful.” Daniel closed her notebook and set it beside the telephone.
Luke looked from the empty station to Jenny. “What are you going to do with her?”
“Keep her comfortable. She’s a reporter, Luke. We need her friend to worry.”
Jenny held his gaze. “He will.”
Daniel smiled and checked the telephone receiver was properly seated.
“Now we wait for the inspector to notice.”
